examples.question_text: Two people of the same mass each consume $2$ standard drinks during a $90$-minute period. One drinks both near the start on an empty stomach; the other drinks gradually after a meal. Explain why identical formula estimates need not mean identical BAC curves.
examples.solution_text:
The formula uses total standard drinks, duration and mass without modelling when each drink is consumed or how quickly alcohol is absorbed.
Food generally slows absorption, while rapid drinking can make alcohol enter the blood faster than it is cleared. Their BAC curves and peak concentrations may therefore differ.
The information does not determine either person's actual peak BAC or whether absorption is complete.

examples.question_text: Two people use the same BAC formula, have the same mass of $72\text{ kg}$ and consume the same alcohol with the same timing. One has a higher proportion of body fat. With other factors equal, explain why their actual BAC values may differ.
examples.solution_text:
Alcohol distributes mainly into body water. Fat tissue contains less water than muscle, so the person with more body fat generally has less body water in which to dilute the alcohol.
With other factors equal, this can produce a higher BAC. The formula gives identical estimates because it does not separately account for body composition; it cannot determine either person's actual BAC.

examples.question_text: A model predicts zero BAC after $4$ hours using $\text{Time}=\dfrac{\text{BAC}}{0.015}$. A person's actual clearance rate is lower than the assumed rate. Explain why the prediction may be too early, and identify another assumption needed for this countdown.
examples.solution_text:
A lower clearance rate means alcohol is removed more slowly, so the same starting BAC takes longer to reach zero.
The countdown also assumes absorption is complete. Continued absorption can cause BAC to remain elevated or rise, invalidating a simple countdown.
The predicted time is an estimate, not confirmation of zero BAC.

examples.question_text: After drinking, a person vomits, drinks coffee and goes for a run. They claim these actions have removed the alcohol and made them fit to drive. Explain the limitations of this claim.
examples.solution_text:
Vomiting may remove unabsorbed alcohol remaining in the stomach, but it does not remove alcohol already in the blood. Alcohol that has reached the small intestine may still be absorbed.
Coffee may change perceived alertness, and sweating is not a reliable way to lower BAC. These actions do not reliably speed up alcohol clearance.
Most alcohol is metabolised by the liver over time. The actions do not establish actual BAC or fitness to drive.

examples.question_text: A regular drinker has a measured BAC of $0.07$ but speaks clearly and says they feel sober. Explain why these observations do not establish fitness to respond to an unexpected driving hazard.
examples.solution_text:
Behavioural tolerance can mask feelings and outward signs of intoxication without lowering measured BAC.
Clear speech and feeling sober do not establish unimpaired attention, judgment or emergency reactions.
Apparent sobriety therefore cannot establish fitness to drive.

examples.question_text: An app reports an estimated BAC of $0.018$. Explain why this result alone cannot establish the person's actual BAC, compliance with an applicable alcohol limit or fitness to drive.
examples.solution_text:
The app uses a model with average assumptions about absorption, distribution and clearance. Individual circumstances can produce a different actual BAC.
A formula estimate is not an alcohol measurement: breath tests measure breath alcohol, while blood tests measure blood alcohol.
Compliance depends on the applicable requirements, including licence category. The estimate also does not measure driving impairment, so it cannot establish fitness to drive.

examples.question_text: A person taking a sedating antihistamine obtains a low BAC estimate after drinking alcohol. Explain why the estimate alone is insufficient to assess fitness to drive.
examples.solution_text:
A sedating antihistamine can cause drowsiness and slow reactions. Combining it with alcohol can increase impairment.
A BAC formula estimates alcohol concentration; it does not measure the combined effects on attention and reactions.
Increased impairment need not involve a change in alcohol clearance. A low BAC estimate therefore cannot establish fitness to drive.

examples.question_text: A person enters $2$ into an app's standard-drink field because they consumed two mixed drinks whose alcohol content is unknown. Explain one input limitation and one separate model limitation affecting the estimate.
examples.solution_text:
Input limitation: one serving may contain more than one standard drink. Counting two servings as $2$ standard drinks can understate intake if the servings contain more alcohol.
Model limitation: even with accurate inputs, average assumptions do not capture every person's absorption, body composition or clearance.
Accurate inputs improve the estimate but do not turn it into a measurement or establish fitness to drive.

examples.derivation: Identical aggregate formula inputs do not specify drinking schedules or absorption rates. Food generally slows absorption; concentrated consumption can increase the rate of alcohol entry relative to clearance. Different curves are possible, but actual peaks and absorption completion cannot be determined from the givens. No numerical calculation is required.

At equal mass, higher body fat generally means less available body water. The same absorbed alcohol distributed through less water can produce a higher concentration. Identical formula inputs therefore need not imply identical actual BAC. The conditional conclusion is appropriate; no numerical calculation is required.

For a fixed starting BAC and completed absorption, time equals concentration divided by clearance rate. A smaller positive clearance rate gives a longer time than the model's four-hour prediction. Continued absorption invalidates this simple countdown. The prediction cannot confirm zero BAC.

Removing stomach contents cannot remove alcohol already circulating, and alcohol beyond the stomach may continue to be absorbed. Perceived alertness and sweating do not establish accelerated clearance. Consequently, the actions establish neither actual BAC nor fitness to drive. No numerical calculation is required.

Behavioural tolerance can reduce subjective and observable signs without reducing the measured concentration. Clear speech and feeling sober do not test attention, judgment or emergency responses. The answer correctly rejects the inference of fitness without claiming a quantified impairment.

An estimate of 0.018 relies on model assumptions and is not a measurement. Breath and blood tests measure different physical alcohol concentrations. Applicable requirements and driving impairment cannot be established by this estimate alone. No universal legal threshold is asserted.

The BAC model estimates alcohol concentration, whereas a sedating medicine can contribute additional impairment. Combined impairment can increase without altered alcohol clearance. A low estimate therefore cannot establish fitness to drive. No numerical calculation is required.

Two servings do not necessarily equal two standard drinks; unknown alcohol content makes the entered value uncertain. Separately, correct inputs cannot eliminate individual differences omitted by average model assumptions. The answer appropriately makes underestimation conditional and distinguishes input uncertainty from model limitations.
